# Material for another lecture

## The three regex engines you keep running into

Almost every language's regex support sits on top of one of three C/C++
libraries.

::: {style="font-size: 0.72em;"}
| Engine    | Origin                          | Algorithm           | Distinctive trait                                             | Used by                                    |
|-----------|---------------------------------|---------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| **PCRE**  | Philip Hazel, 1997 (PCRE2 now)  | Backtracking NFA    | Perl-flavour kitchen sink: lookaround, backrefs, recursion     | PHP, nginx, Git, many C/C++ projects       |
| **ICU**   | IBM Unicode toolkit             | Backtracking        | PCRE-ish syntax **plus** first-class Unicode (`\p{L}`, scripts, locale-aware folding) | R `stringr`/`stringi`, Java, macOS, Swift |
| **RE2**   | Russ Cox, Google, 2010          | Thompson NFA / DFA  | **Linear time guarantee**, drops lookaround and backrefs       | Go `regexp`, Rust `regex`, Code Search     |
:::

- **Backtracking** (PCRE, ICU): expressive, can be exponential on pathological
  patterns (ReDoS).
- **Thompson NFA** (RE2): walks all states in parallel, linear in input length,
  but can't express anything beyond a *regular* language, so no lookaround,
  no backreferences.
- Languages like Python `re`, JavaScript, .NET, and C++ `std::regex` ship
  their own backtracking engines in the same family as PCRE.

## Aside: not all regex engines are the same

The lookahead trick `(?=...)` is not universal. The question is **which
regex engine** the library uses.

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
| Family             | Examples                                              | Lookaround? | Worst case |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|-------------|------------|
| **RE2-style** (NFA) | Go `regexp`, Rust `regex` crate, Google RE2          | **no**      | linear     |
| **Backtracking**   | PCRE, ICU (R `stringr`), Python `re`, JS, C++ `std::regex`, .NET | yes | can be exponential (ReDoS) |
:::

- **RE2-style** trades expressiveness (no lookaround, no backreferences) for
  a guaranteed linear-time match. Built for serving untrusted patterns at
  scale.
- **Backtracking** engines are more expressive but pathological patterns
  (`(a+)+$` on `"aaaa…!"`) can blow up.
- So in Go and Rust, the overlap-counting one-liner doesn't compile. You
  either write the explicit loop, or pull in `regexp2` (Go) or `fancy-regex`
  (Rust), which add lookaround at the cost of the linear-time guarantee.
- The designer's question is *"do I need lookaround?"* and *"do I care
  about adversarial inputs?"*. The agent picks the crate.

## What is ReDoS?

**Regular Expression Denial of Service.** A short input can make a
backtracking engine take astronomically long to decide a match.

The textbook example:

```
pattern:  ^(a+)+$
input:    aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!
```

`(a+)+` can split N `a`s into groups in $2^{N-1}$ ways. The trailing `!`
forces failure, so the engine has to try **every** split before giving up.

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
| `a`s | Time (Python `re`) |
|------|---------------------|
| 20   | ~0.05 s             |
| 25   | ~1.5 s              |
| 30   | ~45 s               |
| 35   | hours               |
:::

Real-world hits: **Cloudflare global outage (2 July 2019)**, a WAF regex
pegged every edge CPU and took the network down for ~30 minutes.
**Stack Overflow outage (20 July 2016)**, a whitespace-stripping regex
on one ~20,000-char post took the site down for 34 minutes.

## Catastrophic backtracking: the mechanism

A backtracking engine tries one branch, fails, backs up, tries another.
Catastrophic backtracking happens when the same input can be matched in
**exponentially many** ways, and the overall match ultimately fails.

The Cloudflare 2019 outage's villain was `.*(?:.*=.*)`, three nested
greedy `.*` quantifiers competing for the same characters.

Walking `abcdefg` (no `=`, so it must fail):

1. The outer `.*` gobbles everything, cursor at end. Need `=`. Not there.
2. Back up one char. Need `=`. Not there. Back up again. Repeat to start.
3. Now the **inner** `.*` tries each split point. For each, the engine
   again searches for `=`. Repeat.
4. Multiply across three nested `.*`s with no anchor between them, and the
   number of partitions to try is on the order of $N^3$.

A few thousand bytes of body with no `=` to anchor on becomes billions of
state transitions. One CPU core, pinned, minutes per request.

## The "evil regex" family

All of these match the same characters in exponentially many ways:

```
.*.*.*          (a+)+          (.*)*
(a|a)+          (\w+\s?)+      ^(a+)+$
```

The fix for `.*=.*` is to **kill the ambiguity** by anchoring:

```
[^=]*=.*        characters-that-aren't-= , then = , then anything
```

Now there is **exactly one** way to split. The engine walks the input
once, in linear time. Same meaning, no backtracking.

This kind of audit is tedious and easy to miss. Which is why Cloudflare
ultimately switched the WAF engine itself to **RE2**, where the bug
class cannot exist.

## Defending against ReDoS

- Avoid nested quantifiers (`(a+)+`, `(.*)*`, `(a|a)+`).
- Anchor and constrain, use character classes instead of `.*` where possible.
- Use **atomic groups** `(?>...)` or **possessive quantifiers** `a++` to
  disable backtracking inside a sub-expression (PCRE, Java, .NET).
- Set a **match timeout** (.NET's `Regex.MatchTimeout`; Go and Rust don't
  need one).
- Bound the length of any user input you feed to a regex.
- For untrusted patterns **or** untrusted input at scale, just use an
  RE2-family engine. That's the whole reason RE2 exists, see
  Russ Cox, *"Regular Expression Matching Can Be Simple And Fast"*,
  <https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp1.html>.

## WAFs: where ReDoS gets really painful

A **Web Application Firewall** sits in front of a web app and inspects
every request for attack signatures (SQL injection, XSS, path traversal,
known-CVE payloads). Each signature is a regex. A real rule set
(OWASP Core Rule Set, ModSecurity, Cloudflare Managed Rules) is hundreds
to thousands of regexes, run against every URL, header, cookie, and body.

WAFs are the worst possible place for a backtracking-pathological regex:

1. **Every request** is matched against **every rule**.
2. The subject is **fully attacker-controlled** (URL, headers, body).
3. Patterns are complex (alternations, nested quantifiers, `.*` everywhere)
   because they have to catch many attack variants.
4. WAFs run on **shared edge infrastructure**, so one bad regex can take
   down many customers at once.

**Cloudflare, 2 July 2019:** a new WAF rule with a nested `(?:.*=.*)`-style
quantifier hit catastrophic backtracking on an ordinary request body.
Every edge CPU worldwide pegged at 100%, global traffic through Cloudflare
stopped for ~30 minutes. Postmortem:
<https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/>.
Cloudflare then migrated their WAF off PCRE onto **RE2**, making that
class of bug impossible by construction.

The lesson: a slow security pattern is itself a DoS vector against the
thing it is supposed to protect.
